             I.​     INTRODUCTION
          Voltus, Inc., (“Voltus”) is a distributed energy resource (“DER”) aggregator operating in

all nine North American wholesale electricity markets. Voltus is a registered curtailment service

provider (“CSP”) with PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., (“PJM”) aggregating the flexible attributes

of retail load across the footprint and offering capacity, energy, and ancillary services products

into PJM markets. Relevant to the provision of capacity, Voltus has participated in all Reliability

Pricing Model (“RPM”) since the Base Residual Auction (“BRA”) for 2022/2023 (held in early

2021) and has delivered its capacity commitments as Demand Resources in the associated

delivery years. Voltus also has experience transacting PJM-accredited capacity bilaterally,

including to support “Bring Your Own CapacityTM” arrangements1. Voltus’s commercial

experience developing demand-side capacity resources closely informs these comments.




1
 See Voltus Blog, Voltus launches “Bring Your Own Capacity Product to Support Data Center Growth and Grid
Resiliency” (Sept. 30, 2025), https://www.voltus.co/press/bring-your-own-capacity-data-centers.

                                                                                                                                           3
         Voltus participated actively throughout the Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) RBP process

and the Connect-and-Manage (“CAM” or “C&M”, IRAS’s predecessor) Senior Task Force

(“CAMSTF”) as well as the merged “CIFP-RBP/CAM.”2 Voltus had earlier engaged in a limited

manner in the preceding CIFP on Large Load Additions (“CIFP-LLA”), which had introduced

several of the concepts carried into the January 17 CIFP-LLA Board Decisional Letter and

same-day White House Energy Dominance Council and PJM State Governors’ Statement of

Principles, which together set the goals and initial shape of the instant tariff filing and the sister

RBP filing now before FERC. Voltus’s comments herein reflect a careful attention to the

evolution of the IRAS (and RBP) frameworks; consideration of the intent of various design

elements and their interactions; and a respect for the challenge of rapidly designing a complex

solution that meaningfully meets an unprecedented moment, while under intense political

scrutiny, and on largely-untested jurisdictional grounds. Voltus’s consistent interest throughout

the stakeholder process has been to ensure a level playing-field for demand-side capacity, with

rules designed to accommodate the differences between various resource classes without

arbitrarily or unnecessarily limiting the ability of distributed resources to address the resource

adequacy shortfall. These comments pick up certain issues Voltus raised during the CIFP process

and seek clarification on new questions raised by the proposed tariff language.

        Voltus contends that incentivizing Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) and

related frameworks is generally more effective and efficient at developing new capacity than

central procurement, and better protects non-cost-causers. Voltus approves the IRAS proposal as

a whole and supports PJM’s reintroduction of the RTO-wide CAM/IRAS incentive framework.

                                                                                                         4
 Voltus     further   appreciates   that   the   framework      includes    demand-side     capacity

resources—Demand Resources (“DR”) and Distributed Energy Resource (“DER”) Capacity

Aggregation Resources—as eligible to support BYONC arrangements, and commends PJM for

responding to broad stakeholder support to include the demand side. Demand-side resource

additions minimize the risk of stranded assets in the face of an uncertain long-term load forecast,

bring revenues directly to retail consumers to offset the increase in energy costs associated with

large load growth, support grid resiliency, and promote the technological and operational

modernization of the grid for more efficient utilization of existing infrastructure, in turn driving

lower system costs and improving affordability. Demand-side resources by definition increase

demand-side flexibility, crucial for absorbing the increasing renewables penetration that is a

policy preference and legislative requirement for many states within the PJM footprint.

         Voltus’s primary concern herein is that by excluding certain critical categories of new,

durable demand-side capacity, the IRAS tariff is unjust and unreasonable because it

unnecessarily limits the volumes of capacity available to ease system constraints and provide

ratepayer relief. This issue is addressed in Section II. Second, Voltus suggests an expansion of

the inclusion of the Peak Shaving Adjustment mechanism to incentivize large load funding of the

same (Section III). Third, Voltus offers minor redlines to clarify and align the required timelines

for reporting and verifying BYONC arrangements (Section IV). A complete set of suggested

redlines is provided in Attachment A.


          II.​   CLARIFYING THE BYONC CRITERIA FOR DEMAND-SIDE
                 RESOURCES     IS   NECESSARY   TO    PREVENT UNDUE
                 DISCRIMINATION, SUPPORT PRIVATE MARKET CONTRACTING,
                 AND PROVIDE A JUST AND REASONABLE RATE
         The inclusion of new capacity from Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation

Resources naturally raises a question as to requirements on the sites underlying the aggregations.

                                                                                                  5
 Stakeholders and PJM staff devoted significant energy to this question during the CIFP process

and discussed the inclusion of several categories: (1) the capacity of sites providing wholesale

capacity for the first time, (2) the added capacity associated with the installation of

behind-the-meter (“BTM”) assets (generation, storage) to support DR/DER participation, and (3)

the potential “reactivation” capacity of sites that supported a capacity resource at some point in

the past, under different conditions, but no longer participate. PJM’s last several proposals on

BYONC eligibility included all three categories, consistent with the analogous allowance of

new-build, incremental, and repowered front-of-the-meter (“FTM”) generation and storage

capacity.

        However, the proposed Tariff language on DR/DER resource eligibility only

unambiguously includes the first category: sites providing wholesale capacity for the first time.

Voltus understands—and there is evidence in the Tariff’s drafting—that excluding both

categories was not the intent: PJM intended preserve the eligibility of new capacity associated

with the installation of BTM generation/storage (“new asset capacity”), but chose to exclude the

“reactivation” of any portion of a site’s capacity not associated with a new asset.3

        Given this understanding of intent, several of the following subsections focus specifically

on site reactivations rather than new asset capacity. Voltus contends that both categories must be

added back to the final tariff and provides a redline to effectuate this change in Section II.E.




3

No. 2222: Fact Sheet (Sept. 28, 2020) (“FERC Order No. 2222 will help usher in the electric grid of the future and
promote competition in electric markets by removing the barriers preventing distributed energy resources (DERs)
from competing on a level playing field in the organized capacity, energy and ancillary services markets run by
regional grid operators.”).

             A.​ For DR/DER Resources, New Assets and Reactivations May Be Ineligible to
                Support BYONC in the New Tariff Language As Drafted
         DR/DER resource eligibility is delineated in proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section

VI(b):

         (ii) For Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources, the resource
         must qualify as a Planned Demand Resource or DER Capacity Aggregation
         Resource, as described in the RAA, Schedule 6 and Schedule 6.2 and:
                (1) be composed of, or reliant on, any location not registered in or prior to
                the 2026/2027 Delivery Year at which an incremental amount at that
                location is the result of the registration of new generation or storage assets
                at the location. However, to the extent three consecutive Delivery Years
                meet the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii), then
                will be composed of, or reliant on, any location registered in the Delivery
                Year prior to the first Delivery Year for which the requirements of Tariff,
                Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) are not met; and/or
                (2) be composed of, or reliant on, locations that were not previously
                supported Capacity Resource, a Peak Shaving Adjustment, or Price
                Responsive Demand for or prior to the 2026/2027 Delivery Year.
                However, to the extent three consecutive Delivery Years meet the
                requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii), then will be
                composed of, or reliant on, locations that were not previously supported a
                Capacity Resource, a Peak Shaving Adjustment, or Price Responsive
                Demand for the Delivery Year prior to the first Delivery Year for which
                the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) are not
                met.
         (The orange reflects text that was included in PJM’s redlined tariff in a different color

than the surrounding text, and may indicate late-stage edits.)

         The second sentences in both VI(b)(ii)(1) and VI(b)(ii)(2) above address the composition

of eligible BYONC in a future state in which the system has left and then returned to the

BYONC posture. Putting these aside for now, DR/DER BYONC resources for the IRAS period

beginning June 1, 2027, must




                                                                                                 7
        be composed of, or reliant on, any location not registered in or prior to the
       2026/2027 Delivery Year at which an incremental amount at that location is the
       result of the registration of new generation or storage assets . . . and/or . . .
       locations that were not previously supported [sic] a Capacity Resource, a Peak
       Shaving Adjustment, or Price Responsive Demand for or prior to the 2026/2027
       Delivery Year.
       The first clause allows new asset capacity but seemingly only at sites with no past

DR/DER participation; the second allows new sites in general. Since sites supporting Capacity

Resources, Peak Shaving Adjustments, and Price Responsive Demand must all be registered in

PJM’s Demand Response Hub database tool (“DR Hub”), the qualification in the second clause

is likely coincident with “not registered” in the first. Additionally, since a new site’s capacity

nomination will count whether or not tied to a new asset, and since the capacity nomination will

include the new asset’s capability, the first clause is redundant to the second. Fundamentally, this

definition counts as new all of (but only the) capacity of never-before-registered sites.

       As to the future IRAS periods, as covered by the second sentences of VI(b)(ii)(1) and

VI(b)(ii)(2), “to the extent three consecutive Delivery Years meet the requirements of Tariff,

Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii),” DR/DER BYONC resources

       will be composed of, or reliant on, any location registered in the Delivery Year
       prior to the first Delivery Year for which the requirements of Tariff, Attachment
       DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) are not met; and/or . . . locations that were not previously
       supported a Capacity Resource, a Peak Shaving Adjustment, or Price Responsive
       Demand for the Delivery Year prior to the first Delivery Year for which the
       requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) are not met.
       On a plain reading, the first clause above actually requires that a site was registered in the

Delivery Year prior to the resumption of the IRAS posture (a requirement at odds with a plain

meaning of “new”), which seems to be the opposite of the intent. Conversely, the second clause

requires that the site was not supporting capacity (and therefore was not registered) in that same

Delivery Year—a more plausible test of “new.” Reading these clauses literally would leave no

path for any site to support BYONC in a future IRAS period. Voltus expects a simple drafting

                                                                                                   8
 error: the exclusion of “not” before “registered” in the first clause. On that assumption, the tariff

is intended to allow reactivations for BYONC in a future IRAS posture, since the test is on

registration and/or support of a capacity product in the year prior to the resumption of IRAS

only.

        Thus the tariff drafting on plain reading allows only new sites today, and (assuming a

one-word addition to resolve the apparent contradiction) both new sites and reactivations toward

BYONC in future IRAS iterations.

           B.​ New BTM Assets and Site Reactivations Are a Genuine and Substantial
               Potential Source of Additive System Capacity
        It is worth considering concretely the assets excluded by PJM’s current definition. First,

without Tariff clarification, new “steel-in-the-ground” physical BTM generation and storage

investments may not support BYONC unless sited at locations that have never before touched a

wholesale capacity product. In parallel, sites that have ever touched a wholesale capacity product

are ineligible. Both exclusions carve away very significant sources of new capacity, and

incentivizing investment in the excluded categories is manifestly good policy, as the following

examples illustrate.

                   1.​ New BTM assets at existing DR/DER sites increase system capacity much
                       like new assets at existing generators/storage projects
        Consider a site that has participated in demand response by changing air conditioning

setpoints, where air conditioning is only 5% of site load at a 20 MW large industrial facility.

Installing a battery on site, sized to meet 95-100% of the full site’s load, will increase the volume

of potential site curtailment by 19 MW. The battery will also add the ability to participate in

ancillary services, the Energy market, and to avoid transmission and distribution system peaks.

Or consider a site already curtailing its full load when PJM’s Emergency Load Response

Program (“ELRP”) is dispatched but with the square footage and appetite to install a solar and

                                                                                                   9
 storage system, fuel cell, etc. that could be reflected as injection capacity under the DER Model.

In both cases, the system gains durable physical infrastructure that is genuinely additive. New

storage and generation installed alongside existing sources of capacity—whether behind the

meter or in front—provide exactly the kind of efficient capacity expansion necessary to

counteract the reliability impacts of unprecedented load growth.

       The BTM placement of new assets provides additional community benefits. BTM assets

improve local grid resiliency, may avoid network upgrades as compared to the generator case for

the same volume of new capacity, and send revenues directly to retail customers. BTM

generation and storage also carry less stranded asset risk than FTM assets because the BTM

assets may have additional use cases, such as providing back-up in the case of a blackout.

                   2.​ GW of capacity capability lie dormant at sites that once participated in DR
       Consider next a location that once did DR but has gone dormant. Perhaps curtailment

proved operationally more disruptive than anticipated, or the facility lost the on-site staff

required to execute a manual reduction when called. As such, the opportunity cost in terms of

production, throughput, or other foregone benefits (e.g. HVAC access) simply exceeded the

compensation the capacity market had to offer. In each case the underlying capability remains

physically present but is “locked out” in absence of a business case sufficient to bring the

capability to market.

       The incentives related to BYONC allow aggregators to overcome these obstacles in

several ways. The aggregator may invest in new systems and equipment—building controls,

automatic load control—that address operational infeasibility. Higher revenues may be sufficient

in themselves to incent participation, and the extended term and revenue certainty associated

with BYONC arrangements may have independent value. In short, BYONC provides the

financial incentive to make the participation of dormant sites feasible and economic.

                                                                                               10
         There are potentially GW of capacity at long-dormant sites. DR, which has been an

eligible RPM resource class since the first auction, in 2007, peaked at just shy of 11 GW

Installed Capacity (“ICAP”) registered Demand Resources in Delivery Year 2015/2016, but was

only 6.76 GW in 2024/20254 (with erosion due to increasing dispatch frequency and other

factors). The delta provides an indication of the volume of existing but “dormant” capability.

Allowing the market to discover these missing GW and their appropriate price is good policy.

Note also that site control upgrades and other investments that may be required to “unlock” the

capability of dormant sites may be accomplished much faster than utility-scale uprates, much

like BTM generation and storage development timelines are shorter than new generator or FTM

storage development timelines. “Modular” distributed investments offer a significant advantage

in terms of Commercial Operation Date (“COD”).

            C.​ Excluding New BTM Assets and Site Reactivations is Undue Discrimination
        Because an assessment of the differential treatment of DR/DER versus generation/storage

resources for BYONC eligibility may be informed by consideration of RBP and Qualifying RBP

Offset (“QRBPO”) criteria, this section notes the resource eligibility criteria for these other two

products as defined in PJM’s companion RBP filing in Docket No. ER26-3380. The same

underlying resources should be able to support both BYONC and QRBPO if tied to load growth

in the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 Delivery Years; this alignment ensures that a zone may receive

QRBPO credit for the capacity investments that are decreasing the zone’s Eligible Large Load

Amount, thus avoiding double procurement.

                       1.​ Treatment of new BTM assets at existing sites versus new capability at
                          existing generators/storage projects
​       Unlike the increase of capacity within an existing generation or storage facility, achieved

in proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VI(a) through either an uprate, the utilization of

additional interconnection rights, or a change to fuel type, all of which are incremental capacity

for an existing physical asset, the addition of new BTM assets involves the addition of

completely new physical assets at an existing site. For this reason, and for those outlined in

section B.1 supra, Voltus’ suggested wording for proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section

VI(b)(ii)(2) captures the capacity related to those new physical assets.

                      2.​ Treatment of DR/DER site reactivations versus generator repowering
        While the "repowering of a deactivated generation resource that deactivated prior to April

10, 2026" is eligible to back BYONC, QRBPO, and even sell offers into RBP itself, a site that

has ever participated as DR in the past is ineligible to support aggregations toward any of the

three products. The proposed Tariff language just quoted applies both to BYONC5 and QRBPO6

resource eligibility. The language on RBP resource eligibility is even more inclusive, allowing

“repowering of a generation resource that had deactivated, or announced deactivation, on or

before April 10, 2026” (emphasis added).7 Given the availability of tests to effectively identify

what DR/DER should be considered eligible to reactivate as new, including the test suggested by

Voltus later in these comments, there is no justification for this discriminatory treatment.

        The exclusion discriminates unduly between rate classes and results in a perverse policy

outcome: native load that constituted the vanguard of DR participation but was subsequently

unable or uninterested in sustaining that participation are blocked from accessing the new large

load incentives that would make market reentry feasible. This will disproportionately affect DR’s

 traditional early adopters, namely commercial and industrial (“C&I”) customers previously

considered “large loads.” Meanwhile, new load can meet its IRAS obligation using on-site load

flexibility backed by storage and generation. The distinction siphons expected BYONC revenues

from veteran to new large loads and promotes on-site asset build-out at data center complexes at

the expense of investment in the efficient utilization of dormant C&I capacity. Early DR adopters

should not be penalized for the long-ago capacity benefits they provided under different market

conditions and DR program designs.

            D.​ In a Context in Which the Private Market Has Been Asked to Proceed
                Expeditiously with Bilateral Negotiations Before Tariff Language Has Been
                Finalized, the Exclusion of New BTM Assets and DR/DER Site Reactivations
                Raises “Notice” Concerns
        This section primarily traces the evolution of the CIFP conversation on DR/DER

reactivation eligibility rather than new BTM asset eligibility, because this is the category that

PJM excluded from both BYONC and QRBPO in its tariff filings. The apparent exclusion from

BYONC of new BTM asset capacity may be a misreading on Voltus’s part or the result of a

drafting error. However, to the extent the category has been excluded, very similar notice

concerns as delineated below apply.

                    1.​ The exclusion of demand-side reactivations contravenes the alignment
                        reached during the CIFP process
        During the CIFP-RBP process and later CIFP-RBP/CAM,Voltus and other stakeholders

advocated that DR/DER site reactivations should be treated as new capacity equivalently with

the generation side. On the BYONC side, Staff included reactivations in its very first proposal

that specified what counted as new DR/DER, presented May 15, 2026.8 All versions of PJM’s

Stage 3 package included reactivations, and PJM staff verbally acknowledged the reasonableness

8

https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/task-forces/camstf/2026/20260515/20260515-item-03a--
-connect--manage-pjm-package---presentation.pdf.

                                                                                                      13
 of providing a market for dormant sites to reactivate as new on the basis of large load price

incentives,   given that existing incentives           had proven        insufficient   for   such sites.

Contemporaneously, BYONC was proposed as eligible to decrement the RBP procurement

target, implying reactivations’ eligibility for this function as well. The tight linkage between

BYONC and the RBP target was maintained until the day before the CIFP Stage 4 meeting.9

                    2.​ Meanwhile, contracting parties made commercial decisions on a
                        reasonable expectation that reactivations would be included
        Thus, for the final six weeks of the stakeholder process, and up until the RBP and IRAS

tariff filings four to six weeks later, stakeholders expected that DR/DER reactivations would be

eligible both to reduce a large load’s IRAS exposure (the BYONC function) and to decrement the

RBP procurement target (the QRBPO function). Given the very short timeframe to finalize

bilaterals, especially for QRBPO purposes, the industry made investments based on the latest and

best understanding of resource eligibility. This meant reactivations on both the generation and

DR sides.

        Pursuing, under conditions of regulatory uncertainty, both the large load bilaterals and the

contracts with the underlying sites that would serve those bilaterals aligned with the best interests

of the system and the provided incentives. Political actors had expressed urgency, and PJM was

actively matching potential buyers and sellers through RBP’s “matchmaking” service.

        BYONC arrangements with potentially very large companies as buyers imply complex

contracting for a product (IRAS protection) never before sold. Parties required time to develop

shared understanding and design agreements addressing risk allocation for unknowns beyond

just present regulatory uncertainty. With IRAS beginning in less than a year and large loads

        Parties were thus encouraged, if not required, to make commercial investments and

pursue commercial arrangements on the basis of evidence-backed assessments as to the range of

final tariff outcomes. As explained above, the DR/DER industry’s defensible expectation was

that site reactivations and new BTM assets would be eligible to supply BYONC.

conclusion nor the justification for discriminatory treatment compared to generators. Neither the

Board CIFP decisional letter10 nor the Board Executive Summaries on RBP11 and IRAS12

mentioned the specific definitions of new DR/DER, and there was no reference to a change in

these definitions or to considerations that would have led to such a change.

            F. Voltus’s Test of Site “Deactivation” is Non-Arbitrary and Non-Gameable
              Resulting in a Just and Reasonable Definition of BYONC-Eligible DR/DER
              Reactivations
                   1.​ What makes an effective deactivation test?
       The inclusion of new sites and new assets as providing new capacity is largely

self-justifying. These resources are providing capacity incremental to the system’s total capacity

today. On the other hand, reactivations—whether of generators and FTM storage or sites

underlying an aggregation—invite further consideration. It is not self-evident that a generator or

site that previously provided system capacity should be counted as new.

       Rather, reactivations provide additive capacity against the counterfactual that the relevant

resource remains out of commission. If a large load incentivizes the resurrection of a resource

that would otherwise stay out of market, that large load may be legitimately credited for

offsetting the impact of its addition. Thus dormant capacity may be considered new again, if the

BYONC arrangement is the cause-in-fact of the repowering. This is the logic supporting

generator repowerings is section VI(b)(i)(4).

       Thus the appropriate definition of DR/DER reactivations must assess whether a site now

out of market would stay out in the normal course of business; in other words, whether it should

be considered actually deactivated rather than temporarily unavailable. A deactivated site is one

that is not out of market for exogenous, short-term reasons such as maintenance, but for reasons

that will hold for the foreseeable future unless there is a material change in market conditions

(such as a sizable increase in available incentives to participate). An effective test will capture

true deactivations as so defined without sweeping in false positives; at the same time, the

line-drawing exercise should not arbitrarily exclude a subset of true deactivations in its efforts to

avoid false positives. Finally, the test should not be gameable. It should not allow for a site, by a



                                                                                                  18
 change in behavior, to intentionally preserve or create the ability to qualify for the BYONC

incentive.

                  2.​ Voltus’s test delivers against the standards just described
       Voltus’s test meets the mark because it calibrates the start of the lookback period to the

specific market conditions of the pre-IRAS Delivery Years. BRAs for both 2025/2026 and

2026/2027 cleared at the administratively-imposed price cap, resulting in unprecedented capacity

value that aggregators could pass on to sites willing to register and perform in these Delivery

Years. BRA results were known well in advance of registration decisions; a retail energy

customer deciding not to participate for those Delivery Years did so with full knowledge of the

high compensation on offer—substantially diminishing the possibility that could have been

incentivized to reenter the market under the non-IRAS status quo. A retail customer with past

experience of DR but that registered in neither of these years has signalled that participation is

uneconomic or otherwise infeasible absent significant changes at the site or with respect to

market conditions. Simply put, if a site that once participated would have come back anyway

absent the BYONC incentive, it would have done so in 2025/2026 or 2026/2027.

       If a site is temporarily unavailable due to maintenance or other ordinary, temporary

conditions, under high pricing conditions, customers and their aggregators are incentivized to

resolve the condition and become available as quickly as possible. Thus, while a single-year

lookback risks sweeping in locations that happened to be unavailable for an ordinary reason but

that would have returned the following year by default, checking for non-registration in

consecutive Delivery Years substantially avoids this risk: a location out for maintenance in

2025/2026 would be expected to return in 2026/2027, and a location out in 2026/2027 would

ordinarily have participated in 2025/2026. Nonparticipation in both years despite the highest

pricing PJM’s capacity market has thus far produced is not readily explained by transient,

                                                                                               19
 addressable circumstances, but instead indicates a permanent choice or necessity to “deactivate”

the site.

        The test is also immune to strategic behavior: when the registration decision for

2025/2026 was made (in May 2025), the IRAS and BYONC frameworks did not exist and were

not reasonably foreseeable in their current form. No location would have withheld itself from the

market in order to preserve or manufacture eligibility for a construct that had not yet been

socialized or developed. The suggested test identifies revealed preference under conditions that

could not have been influenced by the eligibility rule the Commission is now asked to approve.

        Note that pushing back the start of the lookback period does not improve the test but

instead disqualifies true deactivations from 2025/2026. A site whose departure from the market

exactly coincided with a step-change in pricing—an order of magnitude—and which did not

return the following year despite the 2025/2026 price signal and the equally high pricing realized

and available for 2026/2027, should be considered intentionally dormant. Beginning the

lookback with Delivery Year 2025/2026 is a well-justified rather than arbitrary choice.

                   3.​ Voltus’s test solves for other potential concerns
        In conversations with PJM, Voltus has heard another concern that may have informed the

exclusion of reactivations: that Curtailment Service Providers routinely nominate more locations,

and more UCAP, than is strictly necessary to fill a cleared RPM commitment, to build a

performance buffer into the portfolio. Individual locations may effectively cycle in and out of the

resource from year to year or from dispatch to dispatch, such that a location's apparent absence in

a given period does not reflect genuine unavailability. PJM’s concern, as Voltus understands, is

that this “cycling” invites or enables gaming of the “reactivation” category.

        Voltus first observes that there is nothing undesirable about the performance buffer /

cycling dynamic. Aggregators should be encouraged to build redundancy into their portfolios so

                                                                                                20
 they may perform fully against their commitments. Reliable performance across the range of

conditions during dispatch requires portfolio diversification as well as judgment about how to

sequence and manage the participation of individual locations during an event. These activities

are core to an aggregator’s function and comprise the layer converting distributed resources into

a product legible to and usable by the system operator: individually variable end-use customers

may function as a firm capacity resource.

           However, Voltus understands and agrees with the premise of the concern with “cycling”

in the context of reactivation: a location that was available in a given year to contribute to any

test or dispatch, but for whatever reason did not end up doing so, has not deactivated and should

not be counted as new capacity.

           Voltus's recommended test addresses the concern by disqualifying sites that were in any

way available to provide capacity: the test is on registrations, not just participation. Only a

location registered by the start of the Delivery Year may have its actions measured and settled

toward DR/DER performance. Whether the CSP in fact calls upon such location in response to a

PJM dispatch instruction is immaterial: the location was registered, and it therefore fails Voltus’s

reactivation test. The test avoids any “cycling” concerns (as does, incidentally, PJM’s own

proposed wording which defines DR/DER eligibility in terms of registration and/or support of a

capacity resource).

           G. The Proposed Test Provides a Concrete Delineation of Potential Reactivations
              and Is Administratively Viable
       Crucially, Voltus’s test is administratively workable. A time-limited lookback involves a

straightforward, well-defined, and efficient database search against the relevant years’ historical

registrations, with Electric Distribution Company (“EDC”) account number as the identifier. For

PJM verification, lengthier lookback periods introduce data fidelity challenges, the complexity of

changes to the data model over time, and uncertainty as to stability of EDC account numbers: a

given location’s account number may change for a variety of reasons, disrupting database history

for that site. On the customer/aggregator side, there may be insufficient information available to

check eligibility against a longer lookback: a site’s residents, owners, and/or operators may have

no recollection or knowledge of long-past DR participation, or may confuse participation in a

utility DR program carrying no resource adequacy benefits with support of a wholesale capacity

product. A discrete and limited lookback enables customers and aggregators to confidently

assess whether a given site satisfies criteria, providing clarity for bilateral contracting purposes

and greatly reducing the risk that a resource shows up to the Delivery Year partially

“unavailable” for BYONC purposes due to site ineligibility discovered during registrations. In

this situation, large load MW avoided curtailment risk and have been added back to RPM on the

basis of capacity that PJM does not consider to be new. For internal coherence of the

IRAS/BYONC framework, the reactivation test should provide high confidence to all parties as

to a site’s eligibility, so that large loads contracted with DR/DER resources may bring to the

system the expected volume of new capacity as defined.

                IV(b) multiplied by the quotient of [(the sum of all Eligible New Large Load
                Amounts in the Electric Distributor’s zone/area) divided by (the sum of all
                Eligible New Large Load Amounts in the PJM Region)].
 V.​    DETERMINATION OF NEW LARGE LOADS ELIGIBILITY TO PROVIDE
       INTERIM RESOURCE ADEQUACY SERVICE

(a)​    All New Large Loads shall be Eligible New Large Loads to the extent that the sum of a
New Large Load’s Eligible New Large Load Amount is lessgreater than the New Large Load’s
registered peak load (in MW)zero, as provided in the Large Load Registry. New Large Loads
with a cumulative installed capacity equivalent of their BYONC arrangements and assigned
Allocated RBP UCAP MW that equals or exceeds the New Large Load’s registered peak load, as
provided in the Large Load Registry, shall not be Eligible New Large Loads. New Large Loads
that are located within an FRR Service Area cannot be Eligible New Large Loads.

(b)​   A New Large Load’s Eligible New Large Load Amount shall be determined as follows:

       (New Large Load’s registered peak load (in MW), as provided in the Large Load
       Registry) minus (the sum of all BYONC arrangements with the New Large Load
       in accordance with Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VII divided by the Forecast
       Pool Requirement for the first Delivery Year in which the BYONC cleared an
       RPM Auction, plus Allocated RBP UCAP MW assigned to the New Large Load,
       in accordance with Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IX divided by the Forecast
       Pool Requirement for the first Delivery Year in which the Allocated RBP UCAP
       MW cleared an RPM Auction, plus the value of any Peak Shaving Adjustment
       attributed to the Large Load in the Large Load Registry).

(c)​  For purposes of removing its eligibility to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service, a
New Large Load may enter into arrangements with BYONC supported by one or more resources.
 VI.​   BRING YOUR OWN NEW CAPACITY CRITERIA

(a)​   (i) Capacity Resources that cleared an RPM Auction for the first time in the Base
       Residual Auction for the 2027/2028, or 2028/2029, and 2029/2030 Delivery Years or the
       Third Incremental Auction for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year may qualify as BYONC to
       the extent the underlying resource meets the criteria in subsection (b) below.

       (ii)​   Megawatts of Unforced Capacity that have not cleared an RPM Auction, other
       than those specified in subsection (a)(i) above, may qualify as BYONC to the extent the
       underlying resource meets the criteria in subsection (b) below. To the extent three
       consecutive Delivery Years meet the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section
       IV(b)(iii), then megawatts of Unforced Capacity may qualify as BYONC to the extent the
       underlying resource meets the criteria in subsection (b) below and such megawatts (1)
       have not cleared in an RPM Auction conducted for a Delivery Year prior to the first
       Delivery Year for which the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii)
       are not met and (2) meet the eligibility criteria set forth in Tariff, Attachment DD-4,
       section VI.

       (iii)​ With the exception of the RPM Auctions listed in subsection (a)(i) above, to the
       extent megawatts of Unforced Capacity that have cleared an RPM Auction before any
       arrangement with a New Large Load based on such megawatts was reported to the Office
       of the Interconnection, then such megawatts of Unforced Capacity cannot qualify as
       BYONC even if the underlying resource meets the criteria in subsection (b) below.

(b)​     To qualify as Bring Your Own New Capacity, resources must meet the following
eligibility requirements:

       (i)​    For generation and storage resources, the resource must be supported by one of
       the following:

             (1)​    a new-build generation resource including new resources that obtain
                     Capacity Interconnection Rights transferred from deactivated resources or
                     resources that have announced deactivation as of April 10, 2026;

             (2)​    the incremental capacity created by an uprate of Existing Generation
                     Capacity Resources, but only to the extent such incremental capacity is
                     created through an increase in such Generation Capacity Resource’s
                     installed capacity and increase in Capacity Interconnection Rights
                     associated with that Generation Capacity Resource;

             (3)​    the incremental capacity created by the utilization of Surplus
                     Interconnection Service;

             (4)​    repowering of a deactivated generation resource that deactivated prior to
                     April 10, 2026; or
      (5)​     incremental capacity, whether due to greater Unforced Capacity or a
              higher level of Capacity Interconnection Rights, created by an Existing
              Generation Capacity Resource’s changing fuel type to a more efficient fuel
              type.

(ii)​  For Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources, the resource
must qualify as a Planned Demand Resource or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource, as
described in the RAA, Schedule 6 and Schedule 6.2 and must be supported by any
combination of the following:

   (1)​sites never previously registered nor otherwise previously supporting a
       Capacity Resource, a Peak Shaving Adjustment, or Price Responsive
       Demand;
   (2)​new-build behind-the-meter generation or storage assets;
   (3)​reactivations of locations previously registered or otherwise supporting a
       Capacity Resource, a Peak Shaving Adjustment, or Price Responsive Demand
       that deactivated prior to, and were not registered in or since, the 2025/2026
       Delivery Year.
     (1) be composed of, or reliant on, any location not registered in or prior to the
     2026/2027 Delivery Year at which an incremental amount at that location is the
     result of the registration of new generation or storage assets at the location.
     However, to the extent three consecutive Delivery Years meet the requirements of
     Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii), then will be composed of, or reliant
     on, any location registered in the Delivery Year prior to the first Delivery Year for
     which the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) are not met;
     and/or

     (2) be composed of, or reliant on, locations that were not previously supported a
     Capacity Resource, a Peak Shaving Adjustment, or Price Responsive Demand for
     or prior to the 2026/2027 Delivery Year. However, to the extent three consecutive
     Delivery Years meet the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section
     IV(b)(iii), then will be composed of, or reliant on, locations that were not
     previously supported a Capacity Resource, a Peak Shaving Adjustment, or Price
     Responsive Demand for the Delivery Year prior to the first Delivery Year for
     which the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) are not met.
 VII.​ BRING YOUR OWN NEW CAPACITY ARRANGEMENTS WITH NEW LARGE
      LOADS

(a)​   For any BYONC to be in an arrangement with a New Large Load,

       (i)​   the Load Serving Entity serving the New Large Load or the applicable Electric
       Distributor shall report the BYONC in an arrangement with the New Large Load, in
       accordance with the PJM Manuals. The Office of the Interconnection may also accept
       information to the extent interconnection customers, Large Loads, Transmission Owners,
       or other entities voluntarily report any BYONC that may be in an arrangement with a
       New Large Load; and

       (ii)​   the resource owner or entity with contractual authority to enter into a BYONC
       arrangement must certify to the Office of Interconnection, in accordance with the PJM
       Manuals, attesting to the arrangement with the New Large Load and that the BYONC
       will follow the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, sections VI and VIII.

(b)​   For an arrangement between a New Large Load and BYONC to be effective for the
2027/2028 or 2028/2029 Delivery Years, for any BYONC arrangement to be considered, the
requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VII(a) must be met by April 1 for the first
Delivery Year such arrangement is to result in a reduction in the New Large Load’s Eligible New
Large Load Amount. By April 15, the Office of the Interconnection shall update the Large Load
Registry to reflect any verified arrangements between New Large Loads and BYONC.

(c)​    For an arrangement between a New Large Load and BYONC to be effective for the
2029/2030 Delivery Year, for any BYONC arrangement to be considered, the requirements of
Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VII(a) must be reported to the Office of the Interconnection no
later than by 50 days prior to the commencement of the 2029/2030 Base Residual Auction or by
30 days prior to the posting of the planning parameters for the Incremental Auctions arrangement
for the 2029/2030 Delivery Year. The Office of the Interconnection shall update the Large Load
Registry to reflect any verified arrangements between New Large Loads and BYONC after the
relevant RPM Auction.

(d)​    For an arrangement between a New Large Load and BYONC to be effective for the
2030/2031 Delivery Year and subsequent Delivery Years, the requirements of Tariff, Attachment
DD-4, section VII(a) must be reported to the Office of the Interconnection no later than by 30
days prior to the posting of the planning parameters for the relevant RPM Auction for the initial
Delivery Year the BYONC enters into an arrangement with the New Large Load. The Office of
the Interconnection shall update the Large Load Registry to reflect any verified arrangements
between New Large Loads and BYONC after the relevant RPM Auction.

(e)​    BYONC that is in an arrangement with a New Large Load must remain in such
arrangement with that New Large Load unless and until the New Large Load is permanently
out-of-service.

(f)​   A physical resource may support multiple BYONC, each of which may be in an
 arrangement with different New Large Loads, as long as no BYONC is in an arrangement with
more than one New Large Load.

(g)​    A New Large Load may enter into an arrangement with discrete BYONC supported by
different physical resources.

(h)​    A New Large Load may enter into an arrangement with BYONC in excess of its current
Eligible Large Load Amount, e.g., to allow for expected growth in the New Large Load, and the
full megawatt quantity of such BYONC shall be offered in the first RPM Auction for which the
New Large Load is included in the Variable Resource Requirement Curve.

(i)​   (i) For any generation or storage resource, the Accredited UCAP of any BYONC shall
       be the Accredited UCAP for the RPM Auction in which the BYONC cleared for the
       initial Delivery Year the BYONC is in an arrangement with the New Large Load.

       (ii) For Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources, the Accredited
       UCAP shall be the Accredited UCAP for the RPM Auction in which the BYONC cleared
       for the initial Delivery Year the BYONC is in an arrangement with the New Large Load
       and must be demonstrated each year for a 10-year period using the Demand Response or
       DER Capacity Aggregation Resources installed capacity for the first Delivery Year after
       the BYONC is in an arrangement with the New Large Load. For Demand Resources or
       DER Capacity Aggregation Resources that are also the actual New Large Load, there is
       no demonstration required for the initial Delivery Year only to not be an Eligible New
       Large Load.
 VIII.​ BRING YOUR OWN NEW CAPACITY PARTICIPATION IN THE
       RELIABILITY PRICING MODEL

(a)​    All BYONC in an arrangement with a New Large Load must meet the requirements in
Tariff, Attachment DD, section 5.5A and become Capacity Resources eligible to participate in
RPM Auctions.

(b)​   All BYONC in an arrangement with a New Large Load must be offered into the RPM
Auctions as Capacity Resources consistent with and pursuant to the capacity must-offer
requirements and exceptions set forth in Tariff, Attachment DD, sections 6.6 and 6.6A. BYONC
may not seek an exception to the capacity must-offer requirement to provide an external sale, as
available under Tariff, Attachment DD, section 6.6(g) for a 10-year period starting with the first
Delivery Year which the BYONC is in an arrangement with the New Large Load.

(c)​   All BYONC in an arrangement with a New Large Load and committed through RPM
Auctions will be subject to all capacity market rules, as set forth in Tariff, Attachments DD and
DD-1.

(d)​   To the extent the resource supporting a BYONC arrangement:

​       (i) is reviewed by PJM immediately prior to the start of a Delivery Year, or at any other
time, and does not meet the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VI(b); or

​      (ii) is otherwise unavailable in a given Delivery Year,

the seller of such resource will be subject to all relevant deficiency charges under Tariff,
Attachment DD.

(e)​    All BYONC in an arrangement with a New Large Load and not qualifying for an
exception pursuant to Tariff, Attachment DD, section 6.6(g), must be offered into the applicable
RPM Auctions as price takers, i.e., $0/MW-day UCAP for a 10-year period starting with the first
Delivery Year which the BYONC is in an arrangement with the New Large Load. To the extent
the resource is a Demand Resource or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource, the BYONC shall
participate in RPM Auctions for ten (10) consecutive Delivery Years as an Annual Demand
Resource or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource, as applicable; provided, however, the seller of
such Demand Resource or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource may, in accordance with Tariff,
Attachment DD-4, section VII(a)(i) report to the Office of the Interconnection BYONC that
replaces such BYONC, where such replacement shall be for the remainder of the replaced
BYONC’s ten-year RPM Auction participation commitment and the replaced BYONC (and its
supporting registrations) may no longer provide BYONC. In such event, the replacement
BYONC would need to be supported by the certification required by Tariff, Attachment DD-4,
section VII(a)(ii), and such replacement arrangement must be effective coincident with the initial
BYONC releasing its arrangement.

(f)​   To the extent three consecutive Delivery Years meet the requirements of Tariff,
Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii), then any existing BYONC are relieved of the obligations
under this Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VIII.
 IX.​   ALLOCATION OF RBP UCAP MW

(a)​   Each Electric Distributor zone/area allocated RBP Charges pursuant to Tariff, Attachment
DD, section 18.3(a) shall be allocated RBP UCAP MW on a pro-rata basis using the Electric
Distributor zone/area’s assigned share of the total Final RBP Target MW across all zone/areas.

(b)​   Each New Large Load’s Allocated RBP UCAP MW shall be determined as follows:

       (i)​   Each Electric Distributor allocated RBP UCAP MW shall inform the Office of the
       Interconnection how such RBP UCAP MW should be further allocated among the New
       Large Loads located in the Electric Distributor’s zone/area; or

       (ii)​   In the event the Electric Distributor has not informed the Office of the
       Interconnection how its RBP UCAP MW should be further allocated by April 1 before a
       given Delivery Year, the Office of the Interconnection shall allocate such RBP UCAP
       MW to the Electric Distributor’s zone/area pro-rata among all New Large Loads located
       in the zone/area.

(c)​   The Office of the Interconnection shall list in the Large Load Registry each New Large
Load’s Allocated RBP UCAP MW.
 X.​    COMPENSATION FOR PROVIDING INTERIM RESOURCE ADEQUACY
       SERVICE

(a)​     The rate for the provision of Interim Resource Adequacy Service shall be 50% of the
Non-Performance Charge Rate specified in Tariff, Attachment DD, section 10A(e), unless any
Eligible New Large Load elects to (i) accept in its retail rates a sum less than 50% of the
Non-Performance Charge Rate as compensation for the provision of wholesale Interim Resource
Adequacy Service, or (ii) waive receipt in its retail rates any compensation for the provision of
wholesale Interim Resource Adequacy Service as contemplated by Tariff, Attachment DD-4,
section X(c). If any Eligible New Large Load so elects to accept less than 50% of the
Non-Performance Charge Rate or waives in its entirety receipt of compensation for the provision
of wholesale Interim Resource Adequacy Service, the wholesale rate for the provision of Interim
Resource Adequacy Service shall reflect the accepted sum less than 50% of the
Non-Performance Charge Rate or if compensation is waived entirely, the rate shall be zero
dollars.

(b)​   (i) Following an Interim Resource Adequacy Event, unless the Electric Distributor
       informs the Office of the Interconnection otherwise in accordance with Tariff,
       Attachment DD-4, section X(b)(ii), the Electric Distributor shall be responsible for
       compensating all Eligible New Large Loads that provided Interim Resource Adequacy
       Service for up to the amount of such service provided. The Electric Distributor shall be
       responsible for charging customers in its zone/area to fund any such compensation.

       (ii)​   The Electric Distributor may request the Office of the Interconnection to
       compensate certain Members for the provision of Interim Resource Adequacy Service
       and to assess charges on certain Load Serving Entities within the Electric Distributor’s
       zone/area to fund such compensation. In support of such request, as further set forth in
       the PJM Manuals, the Electric Distributor shall (1) identify each Member to be
       compensated and provide the level of compensation and (2) identify each Load Serving
       Entity to be charged and the level of charge.

       (iii)​ The Office of the Interconnection, PJMSettlement, and the Members will not
       assume financial responsibility for the failure of a party to pay any amounts owed to
       another party under this section. In the event the Electric Distributor requests the Office
       of the Interconnection facilitate the billing associated with an Interim Resource Adequacy
       Event, such billing shall be considered a bilateral transaction between the Electric
       Distributor and the identified Members and PJMSettlement shall not be a contracting
       party to the settlement.

(c)​   Nothing in this Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section X shall interfere with any Eligible New
Large Load’s election to (i) accept in its retail rates a sum less than 50% of the Non-Performance
Charge Rate as compensation for the provision of wholesale Interim Resource Adequacy
Service, or (ii) waive receipt in its retail rates any compensation for the provision of wholesale
Interim Resource Adequacy Service.

ATTACHMENT A
SUGGESTED REDLINES TO PROPOSED TARIFF, ATTACHMENT DD-4:
          INTERIM RESOURCE ADEQUACY SERVICE
 I.​    INTRODUCTION

This Attachment DD-4 sets forth the terms and conditions governing the provision of Interim
Resource Adequacy Service. As more fully set forth in this Attachment and the PJM Manuals,
and in conjunction with the Reliability Assurance Agreement:

       (a)​   Interim Resource Adequacy Service is a load reduction service, effective starting
with the 2027/2028 Delivery Year, through which Eligible New Large Loads may be
compensated for providing load reductions requested by the Office of the Interconnection to
maintain system reliability for the purpose of supporting the integration of New Large Loads to
the PJM Region that are not in arrangements with new capacity additions to the PJM Region;

       (b)​    Starting with the 2027/2028 Delivery Year, the Office of the Interconnection may,
in accordance with the Manuals, instruct the implementation of an Interim Resource Adequacy
Service Action prior to calling on Pre-Emergency Load Management Reductions Actions after
determining that available economic real-time supply may not be sufficient to maintain reserves
to meet applicable Reserve Requirements and/or Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits
within prescribed limits and prevent cascading outages;

        (c)​    The Large Load Registry maintained by the Office of the Interconnection,
pursuant to the Reliability Assurance Agreement, shall inform which New Large Loads are
eligible to be called on to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service; and

       (d)​   The Office of the Interconnection shall coordinate with Electric Distributors, and
other Members as appropriate, on the provision of Interim Resource Adequacy Service and the
compensation for providing Interim Resource Adequacy Service.
 II.​   RESPONSBILITIES OF THE OFFICE OF THE INTERCONNECTION

The Office of the Interconnection shall:

       (a)​    maintain the Large Load Registry, pursuant to Reliability Assurance Agreement,
               Schedule 11;

       (b)​    identify Eligible New Large Loads;

       (c)​    determine the megawatt quantity of New Large Loads eligible to provide Interim
               Resource Adequacy Service in each Electric Distributor zone/area for a given
               Delivery Year;

       (d)​    starting with the 2027/2028 Delivery Year, issue an Interim Resource Adequacy
               Service Action based on system conditions; and

       (e)​    request Electric Distributors to direct that a quantity of Eligible New Large Load
               Amounts in their respective zone(s)/area(s) be reduced in accordance with an
               Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action.
 III.​   RESPONSBILITIES OF ELECTRIC DISTRIBUTORS

Electric Distributors shall:

        (a)​   execute the Office of the Interconnection’s directives to implement Interim
               Resource Adequacy Service Actions among the Eligible New Large Loads in the
               Electric Distributor’s zone/area, which is an area within a Zone for which the
               relevant Electric Distributor specifies a separate Obligation Peak Load MW value
               and is a service area of an Electric Distributor that is a separately identifiable,
               geographic area bounded by wholesale metering;

        (b)​   coordinate with the Office of the Interconnection in developing and maintaining
               the Large Load Registry by providing the Office of the Interconnection any
               information or data the Electric Distributor believes appropriate to facilitate an
               accurate Large Load Registry, including applicable state or RERRA retail tariff or
               contractual obligations;

        (c)​   coordinate, as appropriate, with the relevant state(s) or RERRA(s), individual
               Load Serving Entities, and customers served by the Load Serving Entities in its
               zone/area to support transparent, effective, and orderly deployment of Interim
               Resource Adequacy Service; and

        (d)​   implement compensation program consistent with Tariff, Attachment DD-4,
               section X.
 IV.​   DETERMINATION OF MAXIMUM INTERIM RESOURCE ADEQUACY
       SERVICE EACH ELIGIBLE NEW LARGE LOAD MAY PROVIDE IN A
       DELIVERY YEAR

(a)​  All Eligible New Large Loads shall be available to be requested to provide Interim
Resource Adequacy Service by the Office of the Interconnection.

(b)​   The amount of Interim Resource Adequacy Service available to the Office of the
Interconnection may change for each Delivery Year depending on the relationship of the amount
of Capacity Resources committed, through Tariff, Attachment DD, for a given Delivery Year,
and the Eligible New Large Load Amounts.

       (i)​     In the event ([the amount of Capacity Resources committed for a given Delivery
                Year (as determined after the Third Incremental Auction) is less than the PJM
                Region Reliability Requirement determined prior to the Third Incremental
                Auction] divided by the Pool-wide Accredited UCAP Factor) by an amount
                greater than the sum (in MW) of all Eligible New Large Load Amounts, then all
                Eligible New Large Load Amounts is needed by the Office of the Interconnection
                to be available to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service for that Delivery
                Year;

       (ii)​    In the event ([the amount of Capacity Resources committed for a given Delivery
                Year (as determined after the Third Incremental Auction) is less than the PJM
                Region Reliability Requirement determined prior to the Third Incremental
                Auction] divided by the Pool-wide Accredited UCAP Factor) by an amount less
                than the sum (in MW) of all Eligible New Large Load Amounts, then the
                difference (in MW) shall be the cumulative amount (in MW) of Eligible New
                Large Load Amounts that the Office of the Interconnection needs to be available
                to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service for that Delivery Year; and

       (iii)​   In the event ([the amount of Capacity Resources committed for a given Delivery
                Year (as determined after the Third Incremental Auction) equals or exceeds the
                PJM Region Reliability Requirement determined prior to the Third Incremental
                Auction] divided by the Pool-wide Accredited UCAP Factor), then the Office of
                the Interconnection does not need any Eligible New Large Loads to be available
                to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service for that Delivery Year.

(c)​    For each Delivery Year that meets the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, sections
IV(b)(i) or IV(b)(ii), the Office of the Interconnection shall determine:

       (i)​     the total amount of Interim Resource Adequacy Service (in MW) needed to be
                available on a daily basis across the PJM Region for the Delivery Year; and

       (ii)​    the total amount of Interim Resource Adequacy Service (in MW) needed to be
                available on a daily basis in each Electric Distributor zone/area for the Delivery
                Year, which shall be equal to the product of the sum of all Eligible New Large
                Load Amounts needed in the PJM Region pursuant to Attachment DD-4, section
                IV(b) multiplied by the quotient of [(the sum of all Eligible New Large Load
                Amounts in the Electric Distributor’s zone/area) divided by (the sum of all
                Eligible New Large Load Amounts in the PJM Region)].
 V.​    DETERMINATION OF NEW LARGE LOADS ELIGIBILITY TO PROVIDE
       INTERIM RESOURCE ADEQUACY SERVICE

(a)​    All New Large Loads shall be Eligible New Large Loads to the extent that the sum of a
New Large Load’s Eligible New Large Load Amount is lessgreater than the New Large Load’s
registered peak load (in MW)zero, as provided in the Large Load Registry. New Large Loads
with a cumulative installed capacity equivalent of their BYONC arrangements and assigned
Allocated RBP UCAP MW that equals or exceeds the New Large Load’s registered peak load, as
provided in the Large Load Registry, shall not be Eligible New Large Loads. New Large Loads
that are located within an FRR Service Area cannot be Eligible New Large Loads.

(b)​   A New Large Load’s Eligible New Large Load Amount shall be determined as follows:

       (New Large Load’s registered peak load (in MW), as provided in the Large Load
       Registry) minus (the sum of all BYONC arrangements with the New Large Load
       in accordance with Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VII divided by the Forecast
       Pool Requirement for the first Delivery Year in which the BYONC cleared an
       RPM Auction, plus Allocated RBP UCAP MW assigned to the New Large Load,
       in accordance with Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IX divided by the Forecast
       Pool Requirement for the first Delivery Year in which the Allocated RBP UCAP
       MW cleared an RPM Auction, plus the value of any Peak Shaving Adjustment
       attributed to the Large Load in the Large Load Registry).

(c)​  For purposes of removing its eligibility to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service, a
New Large Load may enter into arrangements with BYONC supported by one or more resources.
 VI.​   BRING YOUR OWN NEW CAPACITY CRITERIA

(a)​   (i) Capacity Resources that cleared an RPM Auction for the first time in the Base
       Residual Auction for the 2027/2028, or 2028/2029, and 2029/2030 Delivery Years or the
       Third Incremental Auction for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year may qualify as BYONC to
       the extent the underlying resource meets the criteria in subsection (b) below.

       (ii)​   Megawatts of Unforced Capacity that have not cleared an RPM Auction, other
       than those specified in subsection (a)(i) above, may qualify as BYONC to the extent the
       underlying resource meets the criteria in subsection (b) below. To the extent three
       consecutive Delivery Years meet the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section
       IV(b)(iii), then megawatts of Unforced Capacity may qualify as BYONC to the extent the
       underlying resource meets the criteria in subsection (b) below and such megawatts (1)
       have not cleared in an RPM Auction conducted for a Delivery Year prior to the first
       Delivery Year for which the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii)
       are not met and (2) meet the eligibility criteria set forth in Tariff, Attachment DD-4,
       section VI.

       (iii)​ With the exception of the RPM Auctions listed in subsection (a)(i) above, to the
       extent megawatts of Unforced Capacity that have cleared an RPM Auction before any
       arrangement with a New Large Load based on such megawatts was reported to the Office
       of the Interconnection, then such megawatts of Unforced Capacity cannot qualify as
       BYONC even if the underlying resource meets the criteria in subsection (b) below.

(b)​     To qualify as Bring Your Own New Capacity, resources must meet the following
eligibility requirements:

       (i)​    For generation and storage resources, the resource must be supported by one of
       the following:

             (1)​    a new-build generation resource including new resources that obtain
                     Capacity Interconnection Rights transferred from deactivated resources or
                     resources that have announced deactivation as of April 10, 2026;

             (2)​    the incremental capacity created by an uprate of Existing Generation
                     Capacity Resources, but only to the extent such incremental capacity is
                     created through an increase in such Generation Capacity Resource’s
                     installed capacity and increase in Capacity Interconnection Rights
                     associated with that Generation Capacity Resource;

             (3)​    the incremental capacity created by the utilization of Surplus
                     Interconnection Service;

             (4)​    repowering of a deactivated generation resource that deactivated prior to
                     April 10, 2026; or
      (5)​     incremental capacity, whether due to greater Unforced Capacity or a
              higher level of Capacity Interconnection Rights, created by an Existing
              Generation Capacity Resource’s changing fuel type to a more efficient fuel
              type.

(ii)​  For Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources, the resource
must qualify as a Planned Demand Resource or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource, as
described in the RAA, Schedule 6 and Schedule 6.2 and must be supported by any
combination of the following:

   (1)​sites never previously registered nor otherwise previously supporting a
       Capacity Resource, a Peak Shaving Adjustment, or Price Responsive
       Demand;
   (2)​new-build behind-the-meter generation or storage assets;
   (3)​reactivations of locations previously registered or otherwise supporting a
       Capacity Resource, a Peak Shaving Adjustment, or Price Responsive Demand
       that deactivated prior to, and were not registered in or since, the 2025/2026
